paras: The attempted lynching of Steve Allen took place on the night of Monday, July 2, 1888, when a crowd gathered at the jail in Oxford, Mississippi, to lynch Allen, a Black railroad hand accused of killing his section boss, Hodnett. The sheriff had already moved Allen, and later in July a Holly Springs paper said people were still "determined to lynch this murderer wherever they can find him."

According to the Oxford Eagle, Allen worked on the railroad just above Oxford under Hodnett, who discharged him after Allen cursed him in a quarrel that began that morning, reportedly over fifteen cents. Allen reportedly threatened Hodnett, who got a shotgun for protection, and later shot him from "on top of the cut." The Eagle called this the version "most current in the community" and said it could not write "positively of the true state of the case."

That night, believing Allen had waylaid Hodnett, a crowd gathered around the Oxford jail to lynch him, but the sheriff had removed him to "safer quarters." The would-be lynchers were not identified, though a train was reported to have brought some men from Water Valley.

Later, a false report that Allen was in the Holly Springs jail led a mob to organize at Water Valley, according to the Holly Springs South. The South said the sheriff had "so far kept him concealed." No report of an inquest, a trial of Allen, or arrests of the would-be lynchers was found.

All coverage found ran in the Oxford Eagle, on July 5 and July 19. The Eagle's news report described the killing as done "in the most unprovoked manner" and called Allen "the negro" throughout. It allowed that "There is danger in lynch law" but said that if Allen had waylaid Hodnett, those seeking vengeance "felt justifiable for the attempted lynching." The shorter item mocked the failure, saying the attempt "took the cake" and that "The negro is about the only one rejoicing over the failure." The Holly Springs South, for its part, called Allen "this murderer."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Steve Allen
bases: A crowd gathered at the Oxford jail 'with the view of lynching' Allen, who was accused of killing Hodnett, and a mob was later organized at Water Valley to seek him (A1, A3); no one was killed, so this is an attempted lynching.

Allen was not reached or killed: the sheriff had removed him before the crowd gathered and later kept him concealed (A1, A3); the episode was an attempted lynching by a crowd of unstated size acting on the accusation that he had killed Hodnett (A1, A2).

The jail attempt is reported only in the Oxford Eagle's July 5 issue (A1, A2); the Holly Springs South item reprinted on July 19 (A3) confirms that Allen was sought by mobs but describes a later false alarm, not the jail attempt itself.

accounts.label: Oxford Eagle (community account)
accounts.gist: Allen, discharged after cursing Hodnett in a quarrel over fifteen cents, threatened him and then shot him from the top of a cut; a crowd went to the jail Monday night to lynch Allen but the sheriff had moved him. The paper said this was the version most current locally and that it could not vouch for it.

accounts.label: Holly Springs South
accounts.gist: A false report that Allen was in the Holly Springs jail led to telegraph contact with Water Valley, where a mob organized; the sheriff had kept Allen concealed.

framing.detail: The Eagle said 'There is danger in lynch law' and that it would not do 'injustice to a negro,' but described the killing as 'unprovoked' and said the would-be lynchers felt 'justifiable.'
A one-line Eagle item treated the failed attempt as a joke ('took the cake') and said 'The negro is about the only one rejoicing over the failure.'
The Holly Springs South reported the mob's determination without comment but called Allen 'this murderer.'
